instrument: Current FDA-approved VIVITROL labeling, §1.2
quote: VIVITROL is indicated for the prevention of relapse to opioid dependence, following opioid detoxification (1.2).
note: Current FDA labeling retains an OUD indication. The region says naltrexone can be used, not that it is preferred to agonist therapy for all patients; no later prohibition found.

instrument: FDA NDA018932, original oral naltrexone (REVIA) approval
quote: A dose of 50 mg once a day will produce adequate clinical blockade of the actions of parenterally administered opioids.
part: Naltrexone requires adherence to monthly, long-acting injections.
note: Literal unqualified “Naltrexone requires” is overbroad before publication: oral naltrexone existed already. FDA approval record (https://api.fda.gov/drug/drugsfda.json?search=application_number:NDA018932&limit=1): “submission_type”: “ORIG”, “submission_status”: “AP”, “submission_status_date”: “19841120”; product “dosage_form”: “TABLET”, “route”: “ORAL”. Current oral label confirms daily blockade dosing. Context matters: S59-14 itself acknowledges oral use in limited circumstances; if S58-02 is read as implicitly injectable naltrexone, it remains true. No post-2022 supersession.

instrument: Current FDA-approved VIVITROL labeling, §5.3
quote: To prevent occurrence of precipitated withdrawal in patients dependent on opioids, or exacerbation of a pre-existing subclinical withdrawal syndrome, opioid-dependent patients, including those being treated for alcohol dependence, should be opioid-free (including tramadol) before starting VIVITROL treatment. An opioid-free interval of a minimum of 7–10 days is recommended for patients previously dependent on short-acting opioids.
note: Current label retains detoxification/opioid-free initiation and the 7–10-day minimum; it separately warns of vulnerability for up to two weeks after buprenorphine/methadone. No later change eliminating that minimum found. The quoted threshold is a minimum, not a guarantee of sufficient clearance for every opioid.

instrument: Current FDA-approved VIVITROL labeling, §§4/5.6/7
quote: Naltrexone antagonizes the effects of opioid-containing medicines, such as cough and cold remedies, antidiarrheal preparations, and opioid analgesics (7).
note: The opioid-blockade/general incompatibility part remains in current labeling, with a monitored emergency exception. Unconfirmed: the absolute evidence-status clause “has not been evaluated in persons with concomitant pain and opioid use disorder.” FDA/ASAM searches and current label did not establish either a qualifying later authoritative contradiction or a current exhaustive absence of evaluation; no effective supersession date found. Do not treat this mixed region as definitively current or remove its valid blockade statement.

instrument: Current FDA-approved SUBOXONE labeling, §2.3
quote: To avoid precipitating withdrawal, induction with SUBOXONE sublingual film should be undertaken when objective and clear signs of withdrawal are evident
note: Current standard-induction label retains withdrawal-first advice. The original guideline already explicitly permits low-dose initiation while full agonists continue (S59-04/S59-05, rec06-12-body-extraction.txt:1049–1053); later alternative-induction guidance is not by itself a new contradiction. No withdrawal of standard induction found.

instrument: Current FDA-approved VIVITROL labeling, §5.1
quote: Patients should be alerted that they may be more sensitive to opioids, even at lower doses, after VIVITROL treatment is discontinued, especially at the end of a dosing interval (i.e., near the end of the month that VIVITROL was administered), or after a dose of VIVITROL is missed.
note: Current label retains counseling on reduced tolerance and potentially fatal overdose after discontinuation. No reversal of ASAM/CDC advice found.

instrument: VA Buprenorphine for the Management of Chronic Pain, National Guidance Document, August 2024, pp.1–2
quote: Buprenorphine retains many of the same risks associated with use of full agonist opioids for chronic pain management, yet demonstrates less risk of respiratory depression.
note: Later federal guidance discusses pain prescribing “particularly in the absence of Opioid Use Disorder (OUD)” and supports selected transitions while emphasizing their risks; FDA BUTRANS still has a pain indication. It does not prohibit the CDC’s optional transition absent OUD. No contrary later directive found; reduced risk does not mean no overdose risk.
